blocks.text: Polish has a single past tense. The distinctions English makes with *I did*, *I was doing*, *I have done* and *I had done* are carried instead by aspect: the choice between an imperfective verb (*czytałem*, “I was reading, I used to read”) and a perfective one (*przeczytałem*, “I read it through, I’ve read it”).
How a past form is built
A past form has up to four parts. Take Ania’s *napisałam*, “I wrote”:

The suffix *-ł-* forms the so-called l-participle, which agrees with its subject in gender and number, like an adjective. A person marker (*-m*, *-ś*, *-śmy*, *-ście*) then adds the person. The third person has no marker: *napisała* is simply “she wrote.”
The full paradigm
Here is *być*, “to be.” Every regular verb follows the same pattern once you know its stem.

Two details recur in every verb. In the masculine singular the stem ends in a consonant, so an *e* is inserted before the person marker: *był-e-m*, *był-e-ś*. And before the virile ending *-i*, the suffix *ł* is written *l*: *byli*, *czytali*.
First- and second-person neuter forms (*byłom*, *byłoś*) exist in principle but are confined to literary or playful use, so they are left out above.
Virile or non-virile?
The plural distinguishes groups containing at least one male person (virile, *-li*) from all other groups (non-virile, *-ły*): women, children, animals and things.

items.en: My (male) friends have already been there.
My (female) friends have already been there.

items.pl: Ania i Tomek byli w kinie.
items.en: Ania and Tomek were at the cinema.

blocks.text: One man is enough to make a group virile. That’s why Tomek’s parents *wyjechali* in *Przyjdź do nas na Wigilię*, and why Tomek and the professor *rozmawialiśmy* in *Dzień dobry, mówi Tomasz Lewandowski*.
Whose gender?

In the first person, the form shows the speaker’s gender: a man says *byłem*, a woman *byłam*. In the second person it shows the listener’s: Tomek asks Ania *Byłaś już…?* With formal *pan* and *pani* the verb is third person, so it again follows the person addressed: *Pan był?*, *Pani była?* This is why the learner setting at the top of each lesson changes the forms offered to you.
Finding the stem
For most verbs, drop the *-ć* of the infinitive: *czyta-ć → czytał*, *robi-ć → robił*, *pracowa-ć → pracował*.

blocks.text: Verbs in *-nąć* keep *ą* only in the masculine singular: *zasnąłem*, but *zasnęłam*, *zasnęli*. A few of them drop *-ną-* in the past altogether: *zmarznąć → zmarzł*, *zmarzła*.
Person markers that move

In casual speech the person marker can leave the verb and attach to an earlier word, often a question word or pronoun: *Gdzieś był?* for *Gdzie byłeś?*, “Where were you?” This is informal; in writing keep the marker on the verb. In the conditional, the same detachment is fully standard: *Ja bym zapomniała*.
Which aspect?
With only one past tense, aspect does much of the work English does with tenses.

*…ale nie znalazłem*, “…but I didn’t find it”

The l-participle elsewhere
The same *-ł* form turns up in two other places: in the conditional (*byłbym*, *poszłabym*) and in one of the two ways to form the imperfective future (*będę pisał*, *będziesz pracowała*).
